rules.lint: declaration lint: a flow that commits to Bedrock at its FIRST step -- no review before the irreversible
rules.evidence: v1.3 practice addition; narrative constitution Art. IV.

set27.title: Set 27: Keyboard Primacy
set27.description: Power users should never be forced to reach for the mouse

rules.title: Keyboard Sovereignty
avoid: Hidden keyboard shortcuts
Illogical tab order
Critical actions only accessible via mouse
Tooltip-only shortcut documentation
outline: none on focusable elements
Missing skip links for keyboard users
rules.solution: Every primary action must have a visible keyboard shortcut displayed next to it. Tab order must follow visual hierarchy (left-to-right, top-to-bottom). Arrow keys navigate tables/lists. Enter confirms, Escape cancels universally. Function keys (F1-F12) for mode switching. Shortcuts should be mnemonic where possible (Ctrl+S = Save, not Ctrl+Q). A global '?' key reveals all shortcuts in context. Focus is always visible (a clear ring, never outline: none), tab order follows the visual river, and a "Skip to Content" link appears on focus.
rules.why: The keyboard is the operator's instrument; any critical act that requires the mouse demotes the expert.
rules.lint: html lint: mouse-only clickable div/span; outline:none on focusables; positive tabindex
rules.evidence: v1.3 practice addition; Zin generalizes it to input sovereignty.

set28.title: Set 28: Time & Async Clarity
set28.description: Time as the operator lives it: loading states that inform, and interfaces that respect business time, not machine time

rules.title: Loading State Dignity
avoid: Generic 'Please wait...' or 'Loading...' messages
Spinners for operations under 300ms
No indication of progress for long operations
Blocking entire UI for background tasks
rules.solution: Never show spinners for <300ms operations—use optimistic UI instead. For operations 300ms-3s, show subtle progress indicator with no text. For >3s operations, show progress with context: 'Processing 47 of 200 records' or 'Encrypting document (12%)'. For background tasks, use minimized progress bar at top. Always allow user to continue working—never block entire interface unless absolutely necessary. Failed operations follow Rule 38 (Zero Displacement) for error display.
rules.why: Waiting with information is patience; waiting without it is anxiety.
rules.evidence: v1.3 practice addition.

rules.title: Business Time
avoid: Instant resets after critical actions
Machine-speed transitions the eye cannot follow
Timeouts that ignore operational reality
rules.solution: Interfaces respect business time, not machine time. After a critical action, the result stays long enough to be registered; periods, cutoffs, and deadlines are shown in operational terms; long operations acknowledge the wait.
rules.why: Machines reset instantly; humans need a moment to vibe what just happened.
rules.evidence: Narrative constitution Art. VI; Zin ZUI specification v3.0.

set29.title: Set 29: Declaration Governance
set29.description: The law reaches the declaration layer: what stzw check enforces about norms, flows, and authority. These articles existed in the corpus (as Rules 84 and 88 of an earlier numbering) and were already cited by the linter; this set canonizes them into the constitution of record.

rules.title: Visible State
avoid: Norms that fail without telling the operator why
Error codes where human language belongs
Active filters, pending drafts, or permission constraints the user cannot see
Background operations with no visible trace
rules.solution: If the system knows something important, the user must see it. Every norm carries a MESSAGE a human operator can read; every validation that refuses says why in plain words. Invisible state is a violation — in the UI and in the declaration alike.
rules.why: A user who reasons from state they cannot see has been harmed by the interface.
rules.lint: declaration lint: a norm with an empty MESSAGE -- the operator must see why
rules.evidence: Canonized v1.4 from linter case-law; independently rediscovered in the field (REGLES-UX rule 13).

rules.title: Predictable Authority
avoid: Irreversible commits with no declared actor
Targets claiming roles that governance never declared
Controls that change meaning based on hidden context
Role differences left implicit
rules.solution: No control may change meaning based on hidden context: same action, same consequence; same icon, same intent. In declarations, every step that commits to Bedrock names its ACTOR, and every role a target claims is declared in governance. Ambiguity is operational risk.
rules.why: Ambiguous authority is operational risk; sameness of meaning is how trust scales.
rules.lint: declaration lint: a commit with no declared ACTOR; a role claimed but never declared
rules.evidence: Canonized v1.4 from linter case-law; independently rediscovered in the field (REGLES-UX rule 13).

set30.title: Set 30: The Field Vibe
set30.description: Law forged at 375 pixels: the Restolean kitchen campaign distilled. These rules govern the field/touch vibe — each was paid for by a real failure before it was written.

rules.title: One Action Per Screen
avoid: Screens requiring study before use
Dashboards that answer questions nobody asked
All data visible because it exists
rules.solution: Every screen proposes one clear next action -- a "what now?" the operator can seize in three seconds. Details exist behind intent, not in front of it. If the primary action is not obvious at a glance, the screen failed.
rules.why: A screen with one clear action can be used at a glance, under pressure, in a kitchen.
rules.evidence: Restolean field campaign: 11 live iterations with a working restaurateur, 22 simulated tests.

rules.title: A Sheet Is a Hover, Not a Navigation
avoid: Overlays that navigate away from the page
Sheets that lose the scroll position on close
Backdrops that scroll the page beneath
rules.solution: A sheet or popup hovers over the place the user stands; it never navigates. Closing returns exactly where they were -- same scroll, same context. The backdrop freezes the world; the sheet rises from the bottom, within thumb reach.
rules.why: An overlay that navigates steals the place the user trusted it to keep.
rules.evidence: Restolean field campaign: 11 live iterations with a working restaurateur, 22 simulated tests.

rules.title: Navigation Invariance and the Sacred Back
avoid: Navigation that moves or reflows across screens
Hardware back closing the app mid-task
Back paths that skip or reorder history
rules.solution: Primary navigation keeps its position on every screen of a vibe. The hardware or browser back is an intent: intercept it, honor it, and never let the app close by surprise. Every screen opens from the top.
rules.why: The app must never close by surprise; the hardware back is an intent, not an accident.
rules.evidence: Restolean field campaign: 11 live iterations with a working restaurateur, 22 simulated tests.

rules.title: Zero Horizontal Scroll
avoid: Tables forced into phone lists
Content wider than the viewport
Charts that overflow their canvas
rules.solution: The horizontal axis is forbidden to hide data in the field vibe. Lists are flex rows: amounts and dates unbreakable, names truncate with ellipsis. If a table cannot fit, it is not a table here -- it is a list wearing the wrong clothes.
rules.why: The second axis hides data on exactly the devices that can least afford it.
rules.evidence: Restolean field campaign: 11 live iterations with a working restaurateur, 22 simulated tests.

rules.title: Contextual Defaults
avoid: Opening on 'all records'
Filters reset on every visit
Entry links that dump into unfiltered lists
rules.solution: No view opens on 'everything.' Every list opens pre-filtered to the task's slice -- this week, the pending ones, this supplier -- and a contextual entry opens the exact item, not the list that contains it.
rules.why: 'Everything' is not a view; the task's slice is.
rules.evidence: Restolean field campaign: 11 live iterations with a working restaurateur, 22 simulated tests.

set31.title: Set 31: Intelligence Under Law
set31.description: The agentic era governed: an AI is an actor under the constitution, never an authority above it. Same norms, same audit, same dignity.

rules.title: The Agent Is an Actor
avoid: Agent actions outside the audit trail
Model calls that bypass norms
AI features exempted from the constitution
rules.solution: An intelligent agent participating in a flow is an ACTOR: named in the step, subject to the same validations, norms, signatures, and audit trail as any human. The agent is not a ghost in the machine -- it is a citizen of the same law.
rules.why: An agent outside the law is a ghost; inside it, it is accountable like everyone else.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: Proposals, Not Commits
avoid: LLM output written directly to records
Auto-applied AI corrections
Agent-triggered irreversible operations
rules.solution: Intelligence advises; execution decides. A model's output is a proposal -- rendered as such, reviewable, dismissible -- and becomes a commit only through an authority the declaration names. No prompt reaches Bedrock.
rules.why: Intelligence advises; execution decides -- the commit belongs to a named authority.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: Visible Provenance
avoid: AI-generated text indistinguishable from records
Suggestions styled as facts
Machine edits without attribution
rules.solution: Content produced by a model is marked as machine-made wherever it appears, and the mark travels with it. Provenance is visible state; an unmarked machine sentence is a forged signature.
rules.why: Machine-made content unmarked is invisible state of the most corrosive kind.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: Deterministic Islands
avoid: AI summaries that restate figures
Rounded or paraphrased amounts in explanations
Charts drawn from model output instead of records
rules.solution: Business numbers are quoted from the record, never regenerated by a model. An assistant may explain a figure, link it, or put it in context -- the digits themselves come from the deterministic island, verbatim.
rules.why: A paraphrased number is a different number; business figures are quoted, never improvised.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: The Dignity Contract
avoid: Messages implying user incompetence
Comparisons to other users
Service withheld as pressure
rules.solution: Machine-facing language never blames, shames, or compares. A refusal states the circumstance, not the failure: "current criteria were not met" carries the same fact as "you failed" -- without the insult. Every rejection offers a next step.
rules.why: Software that blames diminishes; the fact can always be stated without the insult.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: The Right to a Human
avoid: Support mazes that end at a bot
Human contact hidden or penalized
Escalation that loses the context
rules.solution: Wherever an intelligent system serves an operator or a customer, a human path is always available, clearly labeled, and free of penalty. Escalation carries the context along; nobody restarts their story.
rules.why: No machine may be the last resort; a person must be reachable without penalty.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: Grounded Proactivity
avoid: Assistants that interrupt on model whim
Unsolicited suggestions during focused work
Proactive notifications without declared triggers
rules.solution: A proactive intervention fires only from a declared trigger -- a norm, a threshold, a schedule -- never from an undeclared hunch. Calm governs what the machine says, not just what it shows; silence is the assistant's default vibe.
rules.why: An assistant that interrupts on a hunch spends attention it did not earn.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: Machine Legibility
avoid: Meaning conveyed only by pixels
Anchors on DOM order or coordinates
Interfaces agents must scrape to read
rules.solution: The interface is legible to machines for the same reason it is legible to screen readers: semantic structure, durable named anchors, declared intents. Accessibility law and agent-interop law are one body of law with two beneficiaries.
rules.why: What a screen reader can operate, an agent can operate; legibility is one law with two beneficiaries.
rules.evidence: The agent flower (stzw mcp), the Zai containment doctrine, and Zin’s human-experience trust design.

rules.title: The Assistant Never Masks the Work
avoid: A floating agent widget with a permanent label eating screen width
An assistant panel that covers the content the operator is acting on
An agent affordance that cannot be dismissed or moved off the work
rules.solution: The agent's calling surface is the one floating affordance an interface may carry, and it earns that exception by being minimal: a small circle with a mark, its name appearing only on hover, its expanded surface never covering the work the operator is deciding about. The assistant is a colleague at the elbow, not a billboard over the desk. Rule 110 keeps everything else out of the air; this rule disciplines the one thing allowed to float.
rules.why: An assistant that hides the work it is meant to help with has inverted its own purpose.
rules.evidence: ZinBank (April 2026): the floating agent shipped as a circle with a permanent 'Assistant ZinBank' label masking the interface; reduced to the circle-Z with the label on hover only.

rules.title: The Generator Ships a Working Thing
avoid: Scaffolding presented as a result
Empty tables and placeholder fields where sample data belongs
A generated app the user must finish before they can judge it
Output with no account of what was generated, why, and how to change it
rules.solution: A generator -- human-driven or AI -- ships artifacts that work the moment they are opened: real sample data derived from the declarations, typed inputs introspected from the entities, a simulator when the target cannot run in place, and an embedded, didactic account of what was generated, why, and how to regenerate it differently. Scaffolding is a promise, not a deliverable; the operator should never have to finish the machine's work to evaluate it.
rules.why: An empty shell teaches nothing and proves less. The generated thing is the argument for the generator -- it must stand up on its own.
rules.evidence: Zin build-target culture: every target ships complete or not at all -- webapp targets open working with data, mobile targets include an HTML phone simulator, CLI targets produce an executable, and each output embeds its own guide. Canonized here as law for every UI generator.
